title: Framing: A Stream Has No Messages In It

questions.question: A serial read returns 7. What does that tell you about how many messages arrived?
options: Nothing, seven is a number of bytes and the stream promises order and nothing else
That one message of seven bytes arrived
That at least one message arrived
That the message was truncated
questions.explanation: It might be half a message, two messages, one byte, or a message with noise in front of it. None of those is an error, and every one of them will happen.

questions.question: Why does a delimiter such as a newline stop working for binary data?
options: Binary payloads contain every byte value, including the delimiter, so it has to be escaped
Binary data cannot contain newlines
Delimiters are slower to scan for
The delimiter would be stripped by the driver
questions.explanation: Once you are escaping, you have written half of COBS and the length of a message depends on its contents, which a length prefix avoids entirely.

questions.question: Why is a corrupted length field worse than a corrupted payload byte?
options: It puts the parser out of step with the stream, rather than producing one bad message
It cannot be detected by a checksum
It causes the sender to retransmit
It is not worse, both lose one message
questions.explanation: One bad byte costs one message. A bad length costs the parser's place in the stream, which is why there is a start byte to resynchronise to.

questions.question: Storage is sixteen bytes and a frame claims a payload of two hundred. What should the parser do?
options: Count it, discard it, and go back to hunting for a start byte
Read two hundred bytes into the sixteen byte buffer
Truncate the payload to sixteen bytes and deliver it
Stop parsing and report a fatal error
questions.explanation: A frame that does not fit is not a frame you understood, so truncating delivers a message that was never sent. The length is a claim from outside that indexes your memory, which is why this gets written up as a security advisory.

questions.question: Why does the parser take one byte at a time rather than a buffer?
options: It cannot be handed a whole message by accident, so the awkward splits are not special cases, and it is the shape an interrupt handler needs
It is faster
A buffer would require allocation
Because reads always return one byte
questions.explanation: A byte at a time and a thousand at a time go down the same path, which is what lets the tests split the input at every position and find the same frame.

questions.question: After resynchronising, the parser produces one garbage frame before recovering. Is the framing wrong?
options: No. A start byte can appear inside a payload, so a false lock is possible and a checksum is what catches it
Yes, the start byte should have been escaped
Yes, the parser should scan backwards
No, and a checksum would not help either
questions.explanation: Framing narrows the problem rather than closing it. Knowing which part of the design is doing which job is the difference between fixing this and adding another start byte.
